svg.text: FIG 02: THÉVENIN & NORTON EQUIVALENCE, 3-CASE MATRIX & TEST-SOURCE ARCHITECTURE
Open-Circuit Voltage Voc • Short-Circuit Current Isc • The 3 Calculation Regimes • Virtual Test Source Method • Negative Resistance Physics

g.text: 1. Thévenin & Norton Duals
Thevenin & Norton Equivalence Theorems
Any linear two-terminal active network can be completely replaced at its load
terminals A-B by either of two mutually dual canonical models:
1. Thévenin Equivalent: Voltage source V_th in SERIES with R_th
2. Norton Equivalent: Current source I_N in PARALLEL with R_N
Fundamental Identity: R_th ≡ R_N and V_th = I_N · R_th = I_sc · R_th
Load Terminal Characteristic Equations
Connecting External Load R_L across Terminals A-B:
I_L = V_th / (R_th + R_L) = I_N · [R_N / (R_N + R_L)]
V_L = V_th · [R_L / (R_th + R_L)] = I_L · R_L
Linear V-I Terminal Characteristic Line:
V_terminal = V_oc - I_terminal · R_th
• Open-circuit condition: I = 0 A ⟹ V_terminal = V_oc = V_th (y-intercept)
• Short-circuit condition: V = 0 V ⟹ I_terminal = I_sc = I_N (x-intercept)
• Negative slope: dV/dI = -R_th ⟹ Internal driving resistance.
Ideal Transformer in Thevenin/Norton Analysis
Ideal transformer with turns ratio N₁ : N₂ = 1 : a (where a = N₂ / N₁):
Impedance Reflection Law across Transformer:
Z_primary = Z_secondary / a² = (N₁/N₂)² · Z_secondary
Z_secondary = a² · Z_primary = (N₂/N₁)² · Z_primary
Voltage & Current Scaling:
V₂ = a · V₁ and I₂ = (1/a) · I₁ (Power S₁ = S₂ = V₁I₁*)
• To find Thevenin equivalent looking into primary:
Reflect all secondary sources and impedances to primary: V_th = V₂/a, Z_th = Z₂/a².
Exam Shortcut: Reduces coupled magnetic multi-mesh circuits into 1 loop!
Source Loading & The Voltage Divider Penalty
When a real non-ideal voltage source (V_th, R_th) drives an external load R_L:
V_L = V_th · [R_L / (R_th + R_L)] < V_th
• Loading Error Ratio: ε = (V_L - V_th) / V_th = -R_th / (R_th + R_L) < 0.
• To maintain terminal voltage regulation > 99%:
R_L ≫ R_th (Requirement: R_L ≥ 100 · R_th)
Current Source Loading Dual:
I_L = I_N · [R_N / (R_N + R_L)] ⟹ Requires R_N ≫ R_L
Ideal Voltage Source: R_th = 0 Ω (Zero output impedance, perfect regulation).
Ideal Current Source: R_N = ∞ Ω (Infinite output impedance, perfect stiffness).
2. The 3 Canonical Calculation Regimes
CASE 1: Independent Sources ONLY (No Dependent Sources)
• V_th = V_oc (Open-circuit terminals A-B, solve via standard Nodal/Mesh).
• I_N = I_sc (Short-circuit terminals A-B, solve for short-circuit branch current).
Evaluating R_th (Fastest Route):
1. Deactivate ALL independent sources (V_s → Short, I_s → Open).
2. Look into open terminals A-B and collapse network via series-parallel
and Delta-Star (Δ ↔ Y) reductions: R_th = R_eq.
Verification Cross-Check:
R_th ≡ V_oc / I_sc (Must match R_eq exactly!)
CASE 2: Independent AND Dependent Sources Present
• Network contains internal controlled sources (VCVS, VCCS, CCVS, CCCS).
DANGER: Cannot use direct series-parallel reduction because dependent sources
CANNOT be deactivated!
Calculation Method A: The Open/Short Dual Method
Step 1: Calculate V_th = V_oc with load removed (all sources active).
Step 2: Short-circuit terminals A-B and calculate I_sc (all sources active).
Step 3: R_th = V_oc / I_sc
Calculation Method B: The Virtual Test-Source Method
Step 1: Calculate V_th = V_oc (all sources active).
Step 2: Deactivate ONLY INDEPENDENT sources (V_s → Short, I_s → Open).
Step 3: Keep ALL DEPENDENT sources active!
Step 4: Connect external Test Source (V_test = 1 V or I_test = 1 A) across A-B.
Step 5: R_th = V_test / I_test
(Method B is faster when calculating I_sc requires complex supernodes!)
CASE 3: Dependent Sources ONLY (No Independent Sources)
The Zero-Excitation Dead State:
• With zero independent excitation, circuit is completely unenergized.
V_th = V_oc ≡ 0 V and I_N = I_sc ≡ 0 A
DANGER: Formula R_th = V_oc / I_sc = 0 / 0 (Indeterminate Form!)
The open/short method fails completely because both numerator & denominator are 0.
Mandatory Solution: Virtual Test Source Method
You MUST connect an external auxiliary excitation across terminals A-B:
Option α: Connect V_dc = 1 V ⟹ Solve for resulting current I_dc.
R_th = 1 V / I_dc
Option β: Connect I_dc = 1 A ⟹ Solve for resulting voltage V_dc.
R_th = V_dc / 1 A
Case 3 Equivalent Circuit Architecture:
• Thevenin model consists of a SINGLE RESISTOR R_th (V_th = 0).
• Represents the driving-point input resistance R_in seen by external world.
3. Virtual Test-Source Architecture
Virtual Test Source: 1 V vs. 1 A Decision Rules
When to Choose 1 V Test Voltage Source:
• When connecting 1 V fixes the terminal node potential immediately (V_A = 1 V).
• Ideal for NODAL ANALYSIS: Conductance matrix branch currents are easily written.
• If controlling variable is a branch voltage in parallel with output terminals.
When to Choose 1 A Test Current Source:
• When connecting 1 A injects an exact known current into the output loop.
• Ideal for MESH ANALYSIS: Outer perimeter current is locked directly to 1 A.
Test Source Step-by-Step Solved Problem
Circuit: 2 Ω resistor in series with terminal, shunt 4 Ω resistor, and CCVS 2Ix:
Step 1: Connect V_test = 1 V source across terminals A-B.
Let current entering terminal A be I_test.
Step 2: Write KCL at node A (Voltage V_A = 1 V):
I_test = (1 V - V_internal) / 2 Ω
Step 3: Relate controlling current Ix to node potentials:
Ix = V_internal / 4 Ω ⟹ Dependent source voltage = 2Ix = 0.5 V_internal
Step 4: Solve simultaneous node equations:
V_internal = 0.4 V ⟹ I_test = (1 - 0.4) / 2 = 0.3 A
Step 5: Calculate equivalent resistance:
R_th = V_test / I_test = 1 V / 0.3 A = 3.33 Ω
• Notice that dependent source increased effective resistance from 2 Ω to 3.33 Ω!
• Series-parallel reduction without test source would have given completely wrong value.
Supernode Analysis for Thevenin Evaluation
When a floating voltage source exists inside an active Thevenin network:
1. Enclose floating voltage source in a closed Gaussian boundary (Supernode).
2. Write generalized KCL for all branches puncturing the supernode boundary:
∑ I_leaving = 0
3. Write auxiliary constitutive KVL equation inside supernode:
V_pos - V_neg = V_source
4. Unknown branch current through the floating source cancels out automatically!
Exam Trap: Resistor in parallel with floating source has zero effect on node voltages!
Quick Test-Source Validation Checklist
✓ Did you kill all independent voltage sources (short circuits)?
✓ Did you kill all independent current sources (open circuits)?
✓ Did you leave ALL dependent sources active?
✓ Did you define I_test as ENTERING terminal A (Passive Sign Convention)?
If I_test leaves terminal A instead, your calculated R_th will have a negative sign error!
4. Negative Thevenin Resistance Physics
Physical Reality: Can R_th be Negative?
• In purely passive networks (resistors only), R_th > 0 ALWAYS.
• In networks with DEPENDENT SOURCES, R_th CAN BE NEGATIVE (R_th < 0)!
Physical Meaning of R_th < 0:
1. Network has internal positive feedback through the controlled source.
2. Instead of absorbing power from an external test source, the internal dependent
source actively DELIVERS power BACK into the test source (I_test < 0 for V_test > 0)!
P_absorbed = V_test · I_test < 0 ⟹ Network DELIVERS power!
Common physical realizations: Op-Amp negative impedance converters (NIC), tunnel diodes.
Stability & Load Constraints with R_th < 0
When a passive load resistor R_L is connected across terminals with R_th < 0:
Total Loop Resistance = R_L + R_th = R_L - |R_th|
Regimes of Operation:
1. If R_L > |R_th|:
Total resistance positive → System is STABLE, finite load current I_L.
2. If R_L = |R_th|:
Total resistance = 0 Ω → Indeterminate / Infinite current (Oscillation threshold!).
3. If R_L < |R_th|:
Total loop resistance is negative → UNSTABLE (Exponentially runaway currents!).
Negative R_th Solved Classroom Drill
Circuit: Terminals A-B connected across resistor R = 5 Ω with CCVS α·Ix in series:
Let controlling current Ix be the current entering terminal A. Then CCVS = 8·Ix.
Step 1: Connect 1 V test source across A-B. Then I_test = Ix.
Step 2: Write KVL around the test loop:
1 V - I_test · (5 Ω) + 8 · I_test = 0
1 V = I_test · (5 - 8) = I_test · (-3 Ω)
R_th = 1 V / I_test = -3 Ω !
Exam Verification:
The dependent voltage source opposes normal IR drop with gain greater than R,
pumping net charge into the terminal: negative driving-point resistance confirmed!
